newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian "Vision" plan wants guided market economy.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian "Vision" plan wants guided market economy.

text.p: A committee working out a blueprint for Nigeria's economy into the next century favours a setup in which market forces are guided in the national interest, a spokesman for the "Vision 2010" plan said.

"What seems to be emerging is that Nigeria needs an economy driven by open market forces but guided in accordance with our national interests," committee secretary Alhaji Ibrahim Ida told a news conference late on Thursday.
Ida said after the eighth meeting of the "Vision 2010" Committee, in the capital Abuja, the work was 80 percent complete.

The committee, established in September 1996 by ruling military strongman General Sani Abacha, hasmore than 200 members, many from the private sector, as well as government officials and traditional rulers.

The committee's stated goal, modelled on similar ideas in Southeast Asia, is to produce concrete steps that Nigeria can take to emerge from the economic doldrums and improve living standards for more than 100 million people.

Reliant crude oil exports, Africa's most populous nation has been in deep recession since 1993, when a wave of strikes and protests followed the annulment of presidential elections by a former military government.
Abacha's tight fiscal policies appear to have lowered annual inflation, which had crept close to three figures, and stabilised the naira currency, but have done nothing to relieve recession.

The 1997 budget disappointed the private sector and the World Bank, who expected a commitment to privatisation of state enterprises and the scrapping of a dual exchange rate, which lets some government branches get cheap foreign currency.
"There is a firm agreement that we need to open up our economy, but it must be guided in the overall interest of our people," Ida said.

When Abacha launched "Vision 2010," he said results would guide annual budgets starting in 1998. But many sceptics, including some committee members, fear he will only go along with the plan if he agrees with it.
Western countries also scrutinise Abacha's programme to restore democracy and hand over to civilian rulers in October 1998. The ifantry general's opponents have also said the plan was insincere.
The committee is expected to finish its work at the end of August with the final document presented to Abacha by the end of September, Ida said.
